title: The History of Life
hook: Life is about 3.5 billion years old, but for most of that time it was just microbes. Animals, plants, and us are latecomers crowded into the most recent slice of deep time.
key_points: Life appeared at least ~3.5 billion years ago, and stayed single-celled for billions of years.
Photosynthetic microbes filled the air with oxygen, transforming the planet.
Complex cells, then multicellular life, then animals arose far later.
Geologic time is split into eras: Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic.
content_html: Stretch the history of life across a single year and humans don't show up until the final minutes. Life is at least about 3.5 billion years old, but for the overwhelming majority of that span — roughly the first three billion years — it consisted entirely of single-celled microbes. Their quiet chemistry remade the planet: photosynthetic microbes released oxygen into an atmosphere that had almost none, an event so transformative it's called the Great Oxidation, and it set the stage for oxygen-breathing life to follow.
extra_html: Complexity came slowly and late. Larger cells with internal compartments appeared, then the first multicellular organisms, and only around 540 million years ago did animals diversify rapidly in the "Cambrian explosion." From there the familiar pageant unfolds: fish, then land plants, amphibians, reptiles, the long reign of the dinosaurs, and finally the rise of mammals after the dinosaurs' demise. Geologists organize this deep time into eras — the long Precambrian, then the Paleozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic — each marked by characteristic life and bounded by major upheavals. Britannica's overview of geologic time lays out how these intervals are defined and reminds us of the central, humbling point: the world of plants and animals we take as "life" is a thin and recent crust on top of an immense microbial foundation.

related.title: How Life Began
related.hook: Before the first living thing, there was only chemistry. Abiogenesis is the idea — and active research — into how plain molecules on early Earth crossed the line into life.

related.title: Mass Extinctions
related.hook: Five times in the past half-billion years, life on Earth was nearly wiped out. Each catastrophe reset the course of evolution — and the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs was only the most famous.

related.title: The Tree of Life
related.hook: Humans, mushrooms, and oak trees share an ancestor if you go back far enough — all life on Earth branches from a single common root.

related.title: T. rex Took 40 Years to Reach Full Size
related.hook: We picture T. rex bulking up fast. A study of 17 fossils says the opposite: the eight-ton predator may have taken about 40 years to reach full size — a slow, decades-long build.

related.title: The Four-Winged Dinosaur That Hunted Early Birds
related.hook: Piles of crushed bird bones from ancient China had no obvious culprit. Meet Jian changmaensis: a four-winged, gliding cousin of Velociraptor that may have hunted Earth's earliest birds.

flashcards.prompt: For most of life's history on Earth, what kind of life dominated?
flashcards.explanation_html: Life is ~3.5 billion years old, but it was microbial for billions of years. Complex multicellular life — including animals — is a recent development.

flashcards.prompt: What planet-changing gas did early photosynthetic microbes pump into the atmosphere?
flashcards.explanation_html: Photosynthesizing microbes released oxygen, the 'Great Oxidation,' which reshaped Earth's chemistry and paved the way for oxygen-breathing life.

flashcards.prompt: What are the major eras of geologic time, from oldest to most recent?
flashcards.back_html: The Precambrian (the vast early stretch), then the Paleozoic, Mesozoic (age of dinosaurs), and Cenozoic (age of mammals, including us).
